extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR professionals, labor economists, policy analysts, and stakeholders reviewing or commenting on the DOL overtime rule and its regulatory impact analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological standards used in the Department of Labor's economic/regulatory impact analysis estimating affected workers, costs, and behavioral responses for the overtime (EAP/HCE) final rule. Includes data treatment, modeling choices, definitions, and calculation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affected workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “affected workers” refers to the population of potentially affected EAP workers who either pass the standard duties test and earn at least $684 but less than the new salary level of $1,128 per week or pass only the HCE duties test and earn at least $107,432 but less than the new HCE compensation level of $151,164 per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine the population impacted by the rule; distinguishes workers by duties-test status and earnings relative to specified thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annualized values discount rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereafter, unless otherwise specified, annualized values will be presented using the 7 percent real discount rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All present-value/annualized calculations in the analysis use a 7% real discount rate unless explicitly noted otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounding and calculation convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers are reported at varying levels of aggregation, and are generally rounded to a single decimal point. However, calculations are performed using exact numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported rounded numbers may not sum exactly to displayed totals due to rounding; use underlying exact numbers for precise calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-time definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time is defined as 35 or more hours per week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is applied consistently in classification and analysis of worker populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of full overtime premium (behavioral model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department uses the term “full overtime premium” to describe the adjustment process as modeled, assuming the demand for labor is completely inelastic—employers make no changes to employees' hours in response to these temporary, unanticipated changes in demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a special case of the fixed-wage model and represents an upper-bound behavioral assumption for hours response when modeling transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight-time wage adjustment rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The straight-time wage adjusts to a level that keeps weekly earnings constant when overtime hours are paid at 1.5 times the straight-time wage. In cases where adjusting the straight-time wage results in a wage less than the minimum wage, the straight-time wage is set to the minimum wage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when modeling employer wage adjustments to offset overtime payments; respects minimum wage floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE duties-test characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCE duties test is used in conjunction with the HCE total annual compensation requirement to determine eligibility for the HCE exemption and is much less stringent than the standard and short duties tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects policy choice that very highly paid employees are more likely to be properly classified as exempt; influences assignment of exemption probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/binomial assignment for exemption status
rubrics_metrics.description: A binominal distribution is frequently used for a dichotomous variable. This methodology assigns exempt status to the appropriate share of workers by taking a random draw from a binomial distribution based on estimated probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assign exempt/nonexempt status probabilistically without manual assignment biasing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model choice for relationship between earnings and exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: For the standard exemption, the relationship between earnings and exemption status is better represented with a gamma distribution; for the HCE exemption the relationship is well represented with a linear function because it is linear at high salary levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gamma distribution chosen because it best fit the non-linear data in prior rulemakings; linear used for high-salary HCE population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topcoding and imputation of high earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning in April 2023 the CPS data are topcoded independently each month and represent the average earnings of the top 3 percent. The Department used the standard Pareto distribution approach to impute earnings above the topcoded value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imputation follows Armour & Burkhauser (2013) Pareto approach to improve estimates of topcoded earnings; affects high-earner estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CPS MORG variables to identify populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Various CPS MORG variables are used for identification: PEIO1COW to identify Federal workers; PEERNHRY identifies workers as hourly or nonhourly; PRERNWA measures weekly earnings; PEHRUSL1 and PEHRACT1 identify regular and occasional overtime workers; GTMETSTA used for other identifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping to CPS variables is central to constructing analytic samples; precise variable usage affects population counts and characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of hourly vs salaried computer employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Some computer employees may be exempt even if not paid on a salary basis: hourly computer employees who earn at least $27.63 per hour and perform certain duties are exempt under section 13(a)(17) and were excluded from the analysis because they are paid hourly; salaried computer workers are included since they will be impacted by this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification follows pay basis and applicable statutory/regulatory exemptions; excludes hourly-paid exempt computer employees from impact estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of fee-basis employees in CPS
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative and professional employees may be paid on a fee basis. Although the CPS MORG does not identify fee-basis pay, they are considered nonhourly workers in the CPS and consequently are correctly classified as “salaried.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows inclusion of fee-basis employees in the salaried/nonhourly analytic population despite CPS limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reweighting and exclusion of zero-earnings or zero-hours respondents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department reweighted for workers reporting zero earnings and eliminated, without reweighting, workers who reported both usually working zero hours and working zero hours in the past week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: demographic/employment characteristics similar across excluded vs included groups; acknowledges potential bias if excluded workers differ in overtime patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of workers with unspecified hour variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The share of all workers who stated that their hours vary (but provided no additional information) is 4.4 percent. To the extent these excluded workers are exempt and work more (or fewer) overtime hours than others, transfer payments and costs may be underestimated (or overestimated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flags uncertainty and direction of potential bias from excluding workers with insufficient hours-variability data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OEWS for wage-rate estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous related rulemakings used the CPS to estimate wage rates. The Department is using OEWS data now to conform with standard practice for the Department's economic analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch in data source intended to align with standard practice; acknowledges possible differences from earlier analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits-earnings ratio source and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefits-earnings ratio is derived from BLS's Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC) data using variables CMU1020000000000D and CMU1030000000000D. As of drafting, 2023 ECEC data were available only through Q3, so the Department continued to use 2022 full-year data to calculate the benefits share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains data vintage choices and that some fixed fringe components (e.g., health insurance) are included in the fringe benefit rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of overhead rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has included an overhead rate of 17 percent to account for potential additional overhead costs associated with the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: overhead likely small since existing employer systems for hourly tracking can be used, but 17% included as acknowledgement of potential additional overhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial cost timing assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifty-two weeks may be an overestimate of the amount of time an employer would incur management costs in Year 1; for affected workers earning below $1,128 but at least $844, employers may not incur additional managerial costs until Jan 1, 2025. Because the Department does not know when employers would make changes, the estimate of 52 weeks is used for the entire population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservative timing assumption used for managerial cost estimates; acknowledges potential overstatement for some workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPS reference-week representativeness for occasional overtime
rubrics_metrics.description: The group representing occasional overtime workers is identified as those with occasional overtime hours in the CPS reference week. Because the survey week is representative, the Department believes the prevalence and characteristics of occasional overtime in the survey week are representative of other weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes week-to-week rotation of occasional overtime workers produces representative estimates across the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit hourly wage calculation and minimum-wage implication
rubrics_metrics.description: The implicit hourly wage is calculated as total weekly earnings divided by total weekly hours worked. Example: workers earning $684 per week would earn less than the Federal minimum wage if they work 95 or more hours in a week ($684 ÷ 95 = $7.20/hr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify small proportion of affected workers whose implicit hourly wage would fall below applicable minimum wage under assumed hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of certain CPS codes and observations
rubrics_metrics.description: WHD excluded nine CPS codes that were not relevant to the analysis (e.g., unemployed persons whose last job was in the Armed Forces; workers not FLSA-covered; codes with no observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removes noncovered or irrelevant categories to focus analysis on covered populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external data sources and crosswalks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department references and uses external datasets and tools—O*NET descriptors, University of Michigan PSID 2019, Census occupational code crosswalks (2002 codes), and various BLS and IRS sources—for constructing samples, descriptors, and industry mappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites specific sources and crosswalks; choice of vintage (e.g., 2002 occupation codes) documented and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of literature uncertainty and elasticities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department uses a general measure of elasticity applied to average wage changes, noting other research estimates larger impacts (e.g., price elasticity of demand for overtime hours as low as −0.5) and that elasticity estimates represent short-run demand elasticities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of literature and selection of elasticity parameters is documented; acknowledges alternative estimates and uncertainty in hours-response modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of Type 2 and Type 4 worker distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Type 2 workers (occasional overtime in survey week) will not see increases in regular earnings to the new salary or compensation levels even if their new earnings in this week exceed those new levels; Type 4 workers see increases in regular earnings to the new salary or compensation levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates worker types for modeling earnings impacts depending on typical vs occasional overtime patterns.
